newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil judges use CVRD sale as weapon against govt.
newsitem.headline: Brazil judges use CVRD sale as weapon against govt.

text.p: A power battle between Brazil's government and the judiciary is playing a large part in the slew of legal challenges that has been delaying the selloff of Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD), lawyers said.

Court injunctions against the sale, which have caused the auction to be rescheduled three times already, have been a judges' weapon to respond to the government's criticism of the judicial system, they said.

"There is a conflict between the judiciary and the federal government. (By granting injunctions) the judges may show their strength and it is CVRD which is paying the price," said lawyer Miguel Reale Junior.
Judges have come under attack for high salaries and privileges that the government wants to eliminate in part through its administrative reform now being discussed by Congress.

The CVRD sale, the biggest in Latin America to date, had been originally scheduled for April 29, but it has been delayed due to a host of legal challenges and is now due to take place on May 5, pending a judge's decision on a government appeal.

The government is trying to get rid of all legal challenges to the CVRD sale by appealing to the Superior Court of Justice (STJ), arguing that all lawsuits against the auction be handled by a single tribunal because of a "conflict of interpretation" in lower courts.

If the STJ accepted the government appeal, all cases would be heard by one court, which the government expects to be the Federal Regional Tribunal of Brasilia whose judge has revoked some 10 previous injunctions.

Lawyers said at least two of the three remaining injunctions against the privatization could have been overturned because they were based on the same arguments as other court orders that had already been revoked by other judges.
"The matter is political rather than legal," said Reale Junior.
The spat between the federal goverment and the judiciary is not new.

Earlier this year the Supreme Federal Tribunal (STF) dealt a severe blow to the government by granting a 28.9 percent pay rise to a group of public sector servants which, if extended to the rest of the civil servants, could cost the government 4.0 billion reais a year.

President Fernando Henrique Cardoso reacted with anger and started a war of words between the judiciary and the government, with leading justices signing a strongly worded declaration warning against what they called a tendency towards dictatorship.
More recently Cardoso urged the judicial system to start thinking about its own reform.

Over 120 lawsuits have been filed across the country against the CVRD privatization. Some 21 court injunctions have been granted but only three still have to be revoked, the National Development Bank (BNDES) said.
Despite the delays, analysts and lawyers are confident that CVRD will be sold off.
"None of the lawsuits will prevent the government from selling the company," said lawyer Alberto Portela. "It is a matter of time."
